A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VISE study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Video-LLM benchmarking, key-frame mitigation experiments, attention analyses, and appendix ablations and cases.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds LLaVA-OneVision evaluation, representation-steering experiments, and supplementary controls and ablations.

M1.justification: v1 proposes key-frame selection alone. v2 retains this procedure and adds calibration-based intervention on decoder activations during inference (Section 5.2; Appendix F). This is a substantial new method component, although the main text specifies fixed-vector subtraction while the appendix specifies activation-dependent PCA-subspace suppression.

E1.justification: Both versions use MSVD, MSRVTT, and NExT-QA, retaining 367 benchmark videos, 6,367 questions, seven sycophancy scenarios, and eight complex-question categories. The additional 100 NExT-QA calibration videos introduce separate sampling within existing coverage, rather than a new domain or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds LLaVA-OneVision (7B) to the benchmark comparisons in Tables 1 and 5 and introduces a stratified random three-frame comparator in Table 7. Existing benchmark models and full-frame comparisons remain, making this a targeted expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces disjoint 100-video calibration, layer/strength selection, and a temporally stratified sampling control. It removes the Overall Score metric and replaces the stated 90%/10% curation mixture with a stringent two-stage filtering description. Its main-text attention comparison changes from two biased prompts to neutral versus biased prompts, although Appendix E.3 retains the earlier protocol; these descriptions do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test semantic selection against random frame reduction, selection-model dependence, key-frame failure on LLaVA-OneVision, and steering-layer and intervention-strength sensitivity (Section 3.1; Appendices E–F). The earlier frame-count sweep remains with its 15-frame condition removed. The three Gemini case studies are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, v2 Appendix C.2 explicitly warns that CRS uses a limited subset of initially incorrect answers and may therefore exhibit statistical noise. This adds a qualitative uncertainty qualification, without introducing run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds LLaVA-OneVision results, steering results including five zero-MSS categories, random-frame comparisons, and layer/strength analyses. Table 1's average changes from 24.74 to 27.78 with the enlarged model set; existing model rows and Tables 2–3 retain their values. v1's misleading-count and Overall Score tables disappear, as does the 15-frame MSS result of 12.63%. Selection overlap and attention-gap reductions are newly quantified.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 and Appendix F add mathematical definitions for activation contrasts, standardized separability, PCA subspaces, and steering transformations. v1's Overall Score definition is removed. MSS, CRS, and attention-score definitions remain mathematically unchanged; the expansion concerns formal constructions rather than new theorems.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the mitigation contribution from key-frame selection to two strategies, claiming that representation steering substantially suppresses sycophancy even in highly susceptible models. Evaluation scope increases from five families/eight variants to six/nine. The central VISE benchmark novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments for prioritizing susceptibility over correction receptiveness and interprets CRS patterns as model stubbornness. It qualifies key-frame effectiveness as architecture-dependent, proposes explanations for LLaVA-OneVision's limited response, and discusses model-specific steering vectors and excessive intervention strength. These extend the earlier visual-grounding explanation and general applicability caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and substantial steering implementation information: separate calibration videos, A100 hardware, selected layers 14/19, a ten-dimensional PCA subspace, and LLaVA-OneVision's preferred alpha of 0.25. It also documents LLaVA's inclusion in local A800 inference and clarifies the neutral key-frame-selection prompt.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to LLaVA-OneVision and Zou et al.'s representation engineering, connecting the new intervention to prior work. It removes introductory citations concerning knowledge editing, reasoning, and personality. The related-work discussion and positioning around video-specific sycophancy otherwise remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: The mitigation narrative is substantially reorganized: the former attention-analysis subsection is condensed into Section 5.1 and developed in Appendix E.3, while steering occupies Section 5.2. Dataset exposition, contributions, and supplementary discussion are rewritten; appendices are reorganized, an LLM-use statement is added, and citations change to author-year style.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figures 1–2, removes v1's key-frame workflow Figure 3, and relocates the retained attention plots as Figure 3. New mitigation, control, failure-analysis, and separability tables substantially revise the displays, alongside removal of two older supplementary tables. Typography and page layout change throughout; case-study figures are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The random-frame control and architecture failure tests address meaningful gaps in v1's evidence for key-frame selection. However, v2 makes steering a central contribution while specifying non-equivalent interventions in Section 5.2 and Appendix F.2.2; its main-text and appendix attention protocols also conflict. These inconsistencies affect reproducibility and interpretation of important claims, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the stronger supplementary evidence.
